result: The study characterized a large pan-European cohort of 1173 children aged 5-12 years from six countries, with comprehensive multi-omic measurements including telomere length (qPCR), DNA methylation (450K array), gene expression (microarray), plasma proteins (Luminex), and serum/urinary metabolites (LC-MS/MS and NMR). Standardized developmental assessments were performed including anthropometry, cognitive testing, and behavioral questionnaires.
evaluation: Claims C1-C5, C59-C73 provide detailed, explicit descriptions of the study population, sample collection protocols, measurement platforms, and developmental assessments. The methods are well-documented with appropriate citations and quality control procedures described in supplementary materials.

result: DNA methylation age was calculated using the established Horvath Skin and Blood clock, while two novel biological age clocks were developed: a transcriptome clock and an immunometabolic clock (combining proteins and metabolites). These clocks were trained using elastic net regression against chronological age, with biological age expressed as Δ age (predicted minus chronological age).
evaluation: Claims C6-C8, C10, C70-C71 explicitly describe the clock development methodology with appropriate citations. The use of elastic net regression and cross-validation for the novel clocks is standard practice, and the Horvath clock is an established method.

result: The newly developed transcriptome and immunometabolic clocks showed strong performance in predicting chronological age in a test set (r=0.93 and r=0.84, respectively) and demonstrated significant longitudinal tracking over approximately 6 months (mean increases of 0.33 and 0.22 years, p<0.001 for both).
evaluation: Claims C11-C12, C78-C81 report validation results with specific correlation coefficients and p-values. The longitudinal validation using paired samples approximately 6 months apart provides strong evidence for clock performance, though the test set sizes are relatively small (N=128 and N=151).

result: Telomere length showed weak correlation with chronological age (r=-0.07, p=0.02). The immunometabolic clock comprised 135 predictors (20 proteins, 79 serum metabolites, 36 urinary metabolites), while the transcriptome clock included 1445 genes. Transcriptome clock genes were enriched in ribosome/ribosome biogenesis pathways and immune-related processes, with borderline enrichment among adult aging genes (p=0.052).
evaluation: Claims C74, C82-C86 provide explicit characterization of the biological age markers. The pathway enrichment analysis is appropriately conducted with FDR correction. The borderline significance (p=0.052) for enrichment among adult aging genes is honestly reported, though this limits strong conclusions about overlap with adult aging processes.

result: After adjustment for chronological age and study center, weak correlations were observed between biological age indicators, with only two significant correlations: telomere length and DNA methylation age (r=-0.06, p=0.04) and transcriptome age and immunometabolic age (r=0.08, p=0.01).
evaluation: Claims C13, C87-C88 report partial correlation analyses with appropriate adjustments. The weak correlations suggest these markers capture different aspects of biological aging, though the very small effect sizes raise questions about biological significance despite statistical significance.

result: Associations between biological age markers and health risk factors showed that higher birthweight was associated with greater immunometabolic Δ age (p=0.0075), smoke exposure with greater DNA methylation Δ age (p=0.018-0.023), high family affluence with longer telomere length (p=0.008), and high social capital with lower DNA methylation Δ age (p=0.048) but higher transcriptome Δ age (p=0.011). Girls had longer telomeres than boys (p=3e-06).
evaluation: Claims C14-C16, C89-C95 report associations from linear regression models adjusted for chronological age, sex, ethnicity, and study center. Most associations are at nominal significance (p<0.05) with only the sex-telomere association surviving FDR correction. The cross-sectional design limits causal inference.

result: All four biological age markers were associated with greater BMI z-score (p-values ranging from 8e-4 to 4e-19, all FDR significant). DNA methylation and immunometabolic Δ age were associated with greater height z-score (p=6e-6 and p=4e-11) and fat mass percentage (p=0.0004 and p=5e-6). All markers except telomere length were associated with greater height at nominal significance.
evaluation: Claims C17-C18, C96-C98 report consistent associations between biological age markers and growth/adiposity measures with strong statistical support (multiple FDR-significant findings). The consistency across different biological age markers strengthens the findings, though causality cannot be determined from cross-sectional data.

result: Immunometabolic Δ age was associated with better working memory (p=0.0036, FDR significant) and reduced inattentiveness (p=5e-4, FDR significant). Conversely, DNA methylation Δ age was associated with greater inattentiveness (p=0.03) and poorer externalizing behaviors (p=0.01), while shorter telomere length was associated with poorer externalizing behaviors (p=0.032), all at nominal significance.
evaluation: Claims C19-C23, C99-C104 report associations with cognitive and behavioral outcomes. The immunometabolic age associations survive FDR correction, while DNA methylation and telomere associations are nominally significant. The opposing directions of effect between immunometabolic age and DNA methylation age are notable and support different interpretations of biological aging in children.

result: Immunometabolic Δ age was nominally associated with increased odds of puberty onset (OR: 1.41, 95% CI: 1.01-1.97, p=0.046) in a subset of children aged over 8 years.
evaluation: Claim C105 reports a nominally significant association with puberty onset, but the analysis is limited by small sample size (N=542) and the association does not survive multiple testing correction. The authors acknowledge this limitation, and the borderline confidence interval (lower bound 1.01) suggests the finding requires replication.

result: The authors conclude that biological aging in children is multi-faceted (based on weak correlations between markers), adiposity is an important correlate of accelerated biological aging (based on consistent BMI associations), accelerated immunometabolic age may be beneficial for child development (based on positive cognitive associations), while accelerated DNA methylation age and telomere attrition may reflect detrimental aspects of biological aging (based on associations with behavioral problems).
evaluation: Claims C24-C28 represent interpretive conclusions drawn from the data. The multi-faceted nature is supported by weak inter-marker correlations (C13, C87-C88). The adiposity conclusion is strongly supported by consistent associations across all markers (C17-C18, C96-C98). The differential interpretations of immunometabolic vs. DNA methylation/telomere aging are supported by opposing patterns of association with developmental outcomes (C19-C23, C99-C104), though alternative explanations are not fully excluded.

result: Associations between biological age indicators and developmental measures/health risk factors were estimated using linear regression adjusted for chronological age, sex, ethnicity, and study center.
evaluation: Claim C9 explicitly describes the statistical approach. The adjustment set is appropriate for the research question, though additional sensitivity analyses adjusting for cell counts and health risk factors were performed and reported.

result: The manuscript provides background on biological aging markers, noting that telomere length shortens with age and is a widely applied marker, high-throughput omics methods have been used to develop biological clocks, age acceleration has been associated with age-related phenotypes and mortality, DNA methylation clocks have been extensively applied with second-generation clocks incorporating clinical data, and clocks developed from different data types (transcriptome, metabolome, proteome) are generally weakly correlated, suggesting they capture different facets of aging.
evaluation: Claims C29-C41 represent background knowledge supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These claims accurately represent the current state of the biological aging field and provide context for the study.

result: The manuscript discusses theoretical frameworks for interpreting biological age in children, including the developmental origins of health and disease hypothesis, life-course models of aging, and competing interpretations of whether age acceleration in children represents beneficial maturation (building biological capital) or detrimental wear-and-tear. Limited prior research exists on biological age in children, particularly using transcriptome, proteome, and metabolome data.
evaluation: Claims C42-C58 provide theoretical background and literature review supported by appropriate citations. These claims accurately represent competing hypotheses about biological aging in children and identify gaps in the literature that motivate the current study.

result: The discussion contextualizes findings within the broader literature, noting that BMI has been consistently associated with accelerated aging in adults, height shows mixed associations with lifespan, previous studies have reported associations between DNA methylation age and behavioral problems in children, telomere length and externalizing behaviors, sex differences in telomere length, and that gene expression patterns in aging adults show similarities to the transcriptome clock developed here. Limitations of training clocks on chronological age are discussed.
evaluation: Claims C106-C128 represent discussion points supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. The authors appropriately contextualize their findings and acknowledge limitations, including the challenge of near-perfect age prediction limiting biological age variation and the need for second-generation approaches incorporating clinical outcomes.
